Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Reed (Redwood SE), Alex Kim (Cerulean CTO), Priya Singh (Cerulean Head of Infra), Mark Li (Cerulean Platform Eng), Sarah Gomez (Product)

Summary (auto):
Short discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance, and multi-region fallback strategies. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Want clarity on SLA, failover behavior, cold start impacts and data residency controls. Agreed next steps: share multi-region runbook, run small benchmark, and provide detailed pricing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood, i'll hand over to jonas in a sec for the deep bits but quick intros?
[00:10] Alex: alex here, cto at cerulean, we run a customer-facing recommendations API that has strict latency targets, thanks for doing this.
[00:18] Priya: priya, we own infra, mostly gcp and a couple regions, latency SLO is 120ms p95 for the inference path.
[00:28] Mark: mark, platform eng, i'll be hands-on if we pilot.
[00:34] Maya: awesome. quick agenda: understand your reliability concerns, map to redwood hosted/dedicated/private options, and discuss fallback/multi-region routing and SLA expectations.
[00:45] Jonas: cool, i'll start with how we think about graceful degradation. redwood's runtime supports model fallbacks, multi-region routing, and tiered capacity. one note, sometimes in docs we shorthand 'Redwood Dedicated' but i've heard it called 'Redwood Dedicatd' in bad transcripts so ignore that typo.
[01:05] Alex: ha, noted. main ask: during incidents we need requests to either fail fast or route to a lower-cost model with minimal impact to p95. we can't have spikes pushing p99 to several seconds.
[01:20] Jonas: makes sense. two primary levers: model variant fallbacks and routing policy. fallback example: primary model rdx-3-large -> if node pool saturated route to rdx-3-medium (quantized) with fallback prompt tags so app can annotate degraded quality. this keeps latency low.
[01:39] Priya: do you do automatic KV/prefix cache warmups when failing over? cold starts are our fear.
[01:48] Jonas: good question. for hosted and dedicated we maintain persistent KV caches per cluster for hot prefixes; across regions we do a best-effort warmup using recent request traces and prefix caching. there is a short ramp (10-30s) for less-hot keys; for private/on-prem we can pre-warm during failover windows via the orchestration hooks.
[02:10] Maya: another piece is routing policy—you can set priorities: region affinity, latency-first, or cost-first. in multi-region mode we do health-check probes and real-time metrics to route. if a region flags degraded, we failover within configured window (default 20s).
[02:28] Alex: 20s is a bit long for us, our UI timeouts are 5s. can you do immediate short-circuit to a stubbed response or a lower-latency model?
[02:38] Jonas: yes, you can configure immediate stub responses (fast fail) or graceful fallbacks. fast-fail returns an application-level code so you can show a lightweight cached answer; graceful-fallback switches model variant. you pick per-route policies.
[02:52] Mark: what about multi-region consistency and data residency—if we route to another region does data leave our VPC? we have to maintain residency for certain customers.
[03:02] Maya: for Hosted we offer region-level deployments and can restrict to specific regions; routing to a different region is only enabled if the route policy allows it. for Dedicated and Private you control the network; Private (VPC) keeps data in your network and uses your KMS. we can also do isolated dedicated pools in a region.
[03:20] Priya: fine—what's the SLA for hosted multi-region?
[03:24] Jonas: Hosted has a 99.9% uptime for the inference API in single-region, and for multi-region setups we provide 99.95% contractual SLA on request availability if configured as active-active with cross-region replication. exact terms are in the SLA doc we will share.
[03:40] Alex: good. are there credits or penalties for misses? we need details for our procurement.
[03:45] Maya: yes, credits are typical—monthly service credits tied to downtime windows. we'll include the SLA excerpt in the packet.
[03:52] Priya: security—during failover do logs/audit trails carry customer identifiers? we need end-to-end traceability.
[04:00] Jonas: audit logs include request ids, route decisions, model variants used, and timestamps. for Hosted we push logs to our control plane and you can pull via API; for Dedicated/Private we can forward logs into your SIEM or a secure bucket. encryption in transit and at rest is default; KMS/HSM integrations available for Private.
[04:18] Sarah: are there compliance artifacts—SOC 2, ISO?
[04:21] Maya: yes, we'll share compliance pack. Hosted has SOC2 currently; Private has additional controls for enterprise.
[04:28] Alex: how does canary / rollbacks work in an incident? we run canaries but worried about a bad rollout increasing error surface.
[04:35] Jonas: we support staged rollouts: traffic splits, canary windows, and automatic rollback on error thresholds. during incidents you can trigger immediate rollback. we also have automatic fallback policies that prefer older model versions if a new model's error rate spikes.
[04:50] Mark: curious about cost tradeoffs—if we use multi-region active-active does that double our compute cost?
[04:56] Maya: it increases cost because you run capacity in multiple regions; we offer intelligent routing with dynamic burst capacity to reduce idle spend, and a multi-region pricing add-on that discounts reserved capacity. we'll include an example pricing sheet.
[05:10] Alex: another thing—do you have throttling and backpressure controls to protect downstream systems?
[05:15] Jonas: yes, per-route rate limits, token quotas, and circuit-breaker policies. you can apply soft-throttles with retry-after headers or hard drop. also we support client-side SDK helpers to gracefully retry with jitter.
[05:30] Priya: ok practical scenario—region A goes down, route flips to region B. what's observable and how do we trace per-request?
[05:38] Jonas: observability: console shows per-region latency, error rates, trace links. each request has a global request id and region hop history — e.g., request-abc -> routed to us-east-1 -> failed -> retried in eu-west-1 with model variant metadata. you'll see those events in the trace.
[05:58] Alex: nice. any chance we can get a sample runbook and the JSON event shape for those traces?
[06:03] Maya: yes will attach runbook and example webhook payloads.
[06:08] Mark: from an ops perspective, how long to spin up additional capacity if there's a sustained surge in traffic?
[06:15] Jonas: autoscale is configurable—cold provisioning in cloud typically 2-6 minutes depending on hardware; dedicated reserved pools can burst into a warm spare pool within 45-90 seconds. for ultra-low latency we recommend keeping a small warm headroom.
[06:30] Priya: what's the time to warm the KV cache on a warm spare?
[06:34] Jonas: warm spare keeps KV in memory for the most frequent prefixes; cold keys still ramp ~15-60s. we can pre-warm specific prefixes if you share the list.
[06:45] Alex: ok, our success criteria for pilot: p95 under 150ms, error rate under 0.2%, seamless failover with less than 2% user-facing degradation. can we hit that with hosted or need dedicated/private?
[06:58] Jonas: likely hosted in multi-region active-active can hit it for many workloads; if you need strict residency or guaranteed headroom at scale dedicated/private is safer. we'll run a benchmark.
[07:10] Maya: we'll propose a pilot: 2-week benchmark, 3 test endpoints, compare rdx-3-large hosted vs dedicated pool, capture latency, failover time, and cost estimates.
[07:20] Sarah: timeline—procurement needs pricing by next week ideally.
[07:24] Maya: i'll share pricing spreadsheet tomorrow. jonas will run benchmark checklist.
[07:29] Alex: any previously reported incidents we can review? examples of multi-region failovers?
[07:34] Jonas: we have non-sensitive incident summaries—e.g., last year we had a region-wide network outage that triggered active-active failover in 18s median with KV ramp to 25s. i'll include sanitized data.
[07:50] Priya: last Q—how do you handle stateful sessions if we use context windows and KV caches across regions?
[07:57] Jonas: session affinity is configurable; for cross-region we replicate KV metadata for active-active models but heavy state is best kept in your side-store and we fetch during inference. we also support sticky routing for session consistency.
[08:12] Maya: ok let's recap next steps. jonas, you'll share benchmark checklist and sanitized incident summary.
[08:18] Jonas: yep.
[08:19] Maya: i'll send pricing + SLA excerpt + compliance pack.
[08:23] Alex: priya will send traffic profile and p95 targets.
[08:27] Priya: yes will do by monday.
[08:30] Maya: perfect. thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the attachments and proposed pilot dates.
[08:36] Mark: thanks.
[08:38] Alex: thanks, bye.

End of call.
